chapter: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
title: Club owners then and now: tin-eared operators blame the band
summary: Horace says earlier nightclub operators were hipper; today's, even in Denver, can't tell if a band is good and blame the band when business drops.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: with our fourth interview, fourth interview. And, Horace, I'd like to ask you -- to begin today, I'd like to ask you a number of questions, basically about -- actually, these are just sort of oddball questions, so we'll hit into them one by one, and some of these things we've covered at various times, but I thought I'd sort of like to get them together here. In fact, just a moment ago we were talking about club owners, and so on, some of the problems you have with club owners, especially those who really don't know music and are only interested in making money and want to exploit the band, you might say, for making money, and if they aren't making money, they immediately blame the band, and they fire it, and you get a new band and constantly churning that way.

Do you feel that this has always been this way, or how was your experience, say like when you first started out with the Collegians? Of course, you were probably touring more at that time, but my main question is how were your relationships with club owners and ballroom owners and so on? How did they operate?

You know, a funny thing, Tom, I'm happy you mentioned this. As I think more about this particular situation, which is a drastic one as far as musicians are concerned, but it seems to me, if I remember correctly, in the past, the nightclub operators in the earlier days of jazz were more hip, you know, than the nightclub operators of

today. Maybe a few of them will hear me say this, and I'll get less work. Nevertheless, it seems to be true, though, that back in the days when the Collegians were traveling around or if we had chance to play, oh, a week's stand or two or three weeks, those nightclub operators seemed to have been on the ball, musically. Either that or they loved the music. They didn't have to do like the current operators in some of the clubs. Even here in Denver we have -- I've played two or three places here in Denver where these nightclub operators seem to have a tin ear --
You know what I mean by that.

-- (unintelligible). They don't know whether you're good or bad. They've got to go around and mingle among their customers and say, well, how do you like them? What do you think about them? What do you think? And you could be swinging like mad or playing like mad, and they don't even know this, and so if a situation occurred where the business dropped off, the first thing they would pick on was the band, by letting them out, and the problem actually didn't exist where the band was concerned. It was the inferior help, like the waiters or the bartenders or one of those things, and it probably would go on for months and months before they would detect this particular thing that was happening in the club and the source of the -- what shall I say -- the lack of having a lot of business, I would say,

you know, and right now that's going on, which is a pathetic the very thing, you know, and the first thing they do, they blame the band or they blame the singers or the entertainers, and I think it's an unfair situation, and that's one of the reasons why I have been a little reluctant to play Denver in a lot of clubs which I could have played.
